Clocks, more than the sun, set the hours at which people work and sleep \citep{hamermesh2008cues}. Daylight saving time (DST) uses this to move an hour of light from the morning to the evening, and whether to keep moving the clock is an open question in many countries. The United States Senate passed a bill making DST permanent in 2022 \citep{uscongress2022sunshine}; the European Parliament voted in 2019 to end seasonal clock changes and leave each member state to choose a permanent time, a proposal still awaiting the Council \citep{europarl2019seasonal}; Mexico abolished DST in 2022 \citep{mexico2022ley}. Brazil, which had moved its clocks every summer since 1985, abolished DST in April 2019 \citep{brasil2019decreto}. Since then, from November to February, the sun has set an hour earlier on the clock in the states where 131 million Brazilians live \citep{ibge2023censo}, and both bringing DST back and banning it have since been studied or proposed \citep{ons2024nota, camara2025pl}. The stakes on the road are large: land-transport crashes killed 37,150 people in Brazil in 2024, 15 percent of them pedestrians \citep{datasus2025sim}, and road traffic kills about 1.19 million people a year worldwide \citep{who2023global}. % national_road_deaths.rds (13_design_descriptives.R): 2024, 37,150 deaths, 15.3 percent pedestrians.

The choice between permanent regimes matters because daily schedules are coordinated: work and leisure are worth more when done at the same time as other people's \citep{hamermesh2008cues}. A clock rule therefore moves the whole society's day relative to daylight at once. Two forces then set its cost on the road. People reduce their exposure to hazards they know about, so the harm one observes is net of that avoidance \citep{neidell2009information}; on the road, the avoidance is travel that moves out of the dark. And drivers do not bear the full risk their driving imposes on others \citep{edlin2006accident}, pedestrians and cyclists among them \citep{crandall1984automobile, white2004arms}. Avoidance limits the deaths a darker evening adds, and the externality leaves drivers avoiding less than the risk to others would warrant. Neither argument says how many deaths remain once travel has adjusted, or whether a brighter morning gives them back. Most estimates of the effect of DST on road safety come instead from the clock changes themselves, comparing crashes in the days or weeks just before the clocks move with those just after \citep{sullivan2002role, sood2007short, smith2016spring, laliotis2023summertime, gillmore2025daylight}. Because work and school keep to the clock, a change moves the light at each clock hour overnight while travel stays at the same clock hours. It also adds a second shock, a night with an hour less or more of sleep. A permanent regime involves no lost sleep, and a change of regime observed over several seasons identifies both quantities.

This paper estimates both from Brazil's abolition. Because DST advanced the clock by exactly one hour, each municipality has, on each summer day, one clock hour in the evening that went from daylight to darkness. It is the hour after sunset in standard time, which was the last hour of sunlight under DST and has been the first hour after sunset since abolition. I compute that hour from the solar position at each municipal seat on each date, and do the same for the hour after standard-time sunrise, which went the other way, from darkness to daylight. A triple difference then compares events in the switched hour in the 11 states that had DST in every summer from 2008/09 to 2018/19 with the same hour in 12 states that never had it, in the summer window against the rest of the year, before and after abolition. Because the switched hour moves with the local sun across places and dates, a regional shock or trend would have to follow the sunset of each municipality to produce the estimate, and the hours on either side, whose light changed only in degree, serve as placebos.

Two independent registers measure the outcome. Death certificates, from the Ministry of Health's Mortality Information System (SIM), record the clock time of death, which is close to the time of the crash for those who die on the road, and cover every public road in the country. The open crash data of the Federal Highway Police (PRF) record every crash its officers attend on federal highways, together with the light conditions the officer saw. The officers' records show that the switched hour did turn dark: after abolition, the share of crashes in that hour that officers recorded at dusk or night rose by 24 percentage points.

In the hour that turned dark, road deaths rose by 29.2 log points, about 34 percent, after abolition, from an average of 110 deaths per summer in the treated states. Deaths and injury crashes on federal highways rose by 54 and 22 log points (71 and 25 percent). These estimates hold under inference that does not rely on asymptotics with 23 clusters, both a wild cluster bootstrap and permutation of the treated states. For road deaths, the season-by-season estimates before abolition show no differential trend. The estimate for the hour that turned dark keeps its size, though not its precision, under an imputation estimator that extrapolates a pre-abolition trend, and it holds without the pandemic seasons and when any single state or season is left out. On federal highways, injury crashes show a trend before abolition, and the estimates for deaths and for injury crashes both shrink once a trend is allowed, so I read those records for the first stage and the mechanism and take the size of the effect from road deaths. The rise is concentrated in the switched hour and the next one, which went from twilight to night; hours whose light did not change, including the middle of the day and the night, where an effect of sleep would also appear, do not rise.

Pedestrians bear most of the increase. They were 12 percent of road deaths in the switched hour before abolition and account for 43 percent of the excess after it: their deaths in that hour more than doubled, a rise of 77 log points (115 percent), against 18 log points (20 percent) for all other road users. Travel responded to light as well. Hourly counts at the federal highway stations of the National Traffic Count Plan show that traffic in the darkened hour fell by about 6 percent; traffic in the morning hour that gained light rose by an estimated 12 percent, but that rise does not pass the permutation test. The risk of an injury crash per vehicle in the darkened hour therefore rose by 29 log points (33 percent), more than crashes themselves.

The morning does not give the deaths back. Road deaths in the hour after sunrise, which gained light, did not change ($-3$ log points, standard error 12). Summing over the hours whose light changed, abolition added 54 road deaths per summer (standard error 20). That count includes only deaths at the scene with a recorded time. Estimated over the whole day, the change is too imprecise (standard error 66) to confirm the count or rule it out. Scaling the estimate to deaths without a recorded time and to deaths off the road, most of them in hospital, raises it to between 67 and 137 deaths per summer. At a value of a statistical life transferred to Brazil's income \citep{robinson2019valuing}, the estimated deaths are worth R\$253 million per summer, and R\$637 million under the broadest scaling. The ministry's technical note that preceded abolition concluded that DST no longer saved electricity \citep{mme2019nota}.

Mexico, which abolished DST in October 2022 everywhere except along its northern border, shows the same pattern in the accident register of its national statistics office (INEGI), which covers the roads outside federal jurisdiction, in urban and suburban areas. In the areas that lost DST, deaths at the scene in the hour after standard-time sunset rose by 58 log points (79 percent) relative to hours of the same day whose light did not change, and pedestrian deaths rose most. The Mexican areas that kept their clocks are few and small, so the Mexican estimate rests on this within-day comparison rather than on the triple difference.

The paper contributes to three literatures. The first estimates the effect of DST on road safety, mostly by comparing the days or weeks just before and after the clocks change: in the United States \citep{sood2007short, smith2016spring}, Greece \citep{laliotis2023summertime}, Chile \citep{gillmore2025daylight}, Brazil \citep{franco2023daylight} and Mexico \citep{goodwin2024impact}. They attribute the deaths that follow the spring change to lost sleep \citep{smith2016spring, gillmore2025daylight}, and find that the light DST adds to the evening lowers serious crashes \citep{laliotis2023summertime, gillmore2025daylight} or mainly moves deaths between hours of the day \citep{smith2016spring}. Even a study that asks whether DST should be abolished answers from the transitions \citep{depalo2023should}. Closest to the question of regimes, \citet{bunnings2021spring} estimate the effect of darkness on crashes in Great Britain from the variation in sunrise and sunset times across places and dates, and simulate that year-round DST would save 8 percent of the cost of darkness. \citet{coate2004effects} estimate that year-round DST would avoid 171 pedestrian deaths a year in the United States. This paper observes a change of regime instead of simulating one, over five seasons, with a first stage recorded by third parties. It also locates the deaths in the evening hour and among pedestrians, the road users whose crash risk is most sensitive to ambient light \citep{sullivan2002role, woods2025daylight}, down to the brightness of the moon \citep{tyndall2025road}.

The second literature uses DST to identify the effect of ambient light on behavior, mostly crime \citep{doleac2015under, tealde2022unequal, dominguez2023crime}; in Brazil, homicides by firearm fell during the months of DST, mostly in the early-evening hours that DST lit \citep{toro2016daylight}. These studies, like this one, look for the effect in the hours whose light the clock moves. What differs here is that the shift of light is permanent and arrives without any change in sleep at the moment of the shift.

The third literature weighs the costs and benefits of DST. The items it has measured are mostly energy use \citep{kellogg2008daylight, kotchen2011does} and, through sleep, health and productivity \citep{gibson2018time, giuntella2019sunset}. The road-safety studies above measure mostly the transitions, which a choice between permanent regimes removes either way. This paper adds the road deaths of the regime itself and values them in Section~\ref{sec:cost}.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} describes Brazil's DST and its abolition, Section~\ref{sec:data} the data and Section~\ref{sec:design} the design. Section~\ref{sec:results} reports the results, Section~\ref{sec:cost} their cost and Section~\ref{sec:mexico} the Mexican abolition. Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Daylight Saving Time in Brazil and Its Abolition}\label{sec:background}

\subsection{The policy}

Brazil observed DST in every summer from 1985/86 to 2018/19. The states covered changed often in the 1990s; from 2008 a standing decree fixed both the dates and the states \citep{brasil2008decreto}. Clocks moved forward at midnight on the third Sunday of October (from 2018, the first Sunday of November; \citealp{brasil2017decreto}) and back on the third Sunday of February, a week later when that Sunday fell on Carnival. DST applied in Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Paran\'a, S\~ao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Esp\'irito Santo, Minas Gerais, Goi\'as, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul and the Federal District, which held 131 million of Brazil's 203 million people in 2022 \citep{ibge2023censo}. Within the sample, Bahia had DST only in 2011/12 and Tocantins only in 2012/13. The North and the rest of the Northeast, close to the equator, where the length of the day varies little over the year, did not have DST in this period. Figure~\ref{fig:map} maps the groups.

Decree 9,772 of 25 April 2019 ended DST in the whole country \citep{brasil2019decreto}. It followed a technical note of the Ministry of Mines and Energy which concluded that DST had stopped delivering the electricity savings it was designed for \citep{mme2019nota}. By the ministry's estimate, the 2018/19 season had raised electricity load by about 0.7 percent: savings on evening lighting were outweighed by higher consumption late at night, which the note attributed tentatively to air-conditioning. The question did not close. In 2024 the national grid operator estimated that reinstating DST would lower the evening peak, which rooftop solar generation has made the binding constraint on the system, and save R\$244 to 356 million in thermal-generation fuel in one summer \citep{ons2024nota}. In 2025 a committee of the Chamber of Deputies approved a bill that would forbid DST except, temporarily and regionally, in an energy crisis \citep{camara2025pl}.

\subsection{What abolition changed}

DST adds no light to the day; it moves the clock. Panel A of Figure~\ref{fig:light} shows the clock time of sunset and sunrise in S\~ao Paulo over 2018/19, under the DST then in force and without it. In mid-January the sun set at 7:58 p.m.\ on the clock under DST and now sets at 6:58 p.m.; it rose at 6:32 a.m.\ and now rises at 5:32 a.m. % São Paulo, 15 January, NOAA equations (EXPLICANDO_O_PROJETO.md, section 1.2).
Because work, school and the commute keep to the clock, abolition put the people who used to travel in the last hour of sunlight on the road after sunset.

Let $s_{md}$ be the clock time of sunset in standard time at municipality $m$ on day $d$. Under DST the clock ran an hour ahead, so the sun set at clock time $s_{md}+60$ minutes and was above the horizon throughout the clock hour $[s_{md}, s_{md}+60)$. Since abolition the sun has been below the horizon throughout that hour. I call it hour 0, or the hour that turned dark. Its morning counterpart, the hour after standard-time sunrise $[r_{md}, r_{md}+60)$, was dark under DST and is light now. The neighboring hours changed less: the hour before $s_{md}$ went from full sun to low sun, and the hour after $s_{md}+60$ from twilight to night.

Abolition also involved no transition night. DST ended on 17 February 2019 as scheduled and did not start again in November 2019, so nobody lost an hour of sleep because of abolition. What changed for the rest of every summer was the clock time of sunset.

\section{Data}\label{sec:data}

\subsection{Deaths on the road}

The Mortality Information System (Sistema de Informa\c{c}\~oes sobre Mortalidade, SIM) of the Ministry of Health holds every death certificate issued in Brazil, with the underlying cause of death coded in the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision (ICD-10), the municipality and type of place of occurrence, and the date and clock time of death \citep{datasus2025sim}. I select deaths from land-transport crashes (codes V01--V89) that occurred on a public road and call them road deaths. For a person who dies at the scene, the time of death is close to the time of the crash; for a person who dies in hospital, it may be hours or days later. Deaths in hospital therefore never enter an hourly count. Between 15 and 20 percent of road deaths, depending on the group of states, the time of year and the period, have no clock time and drop out of every count as well. % pretrends.rds, missing_hour: 15.4 to 20.1 percent by group, window and period.
In the treated states, an average summer window before abolition had 2,382 road deaths with a clock time, 110 of them in hour 0 (Table~\ref{tab:descriptives}).

The death register is the standard source on mortality in Brazil, including in economics \citep[for example,][who measure homicide with it]{dixcarneiro2018economic}, and its coverage rests on a legal requirement: no burial may take place without a death record, which the registry office issues on the basis of a physician's death certificate where a physician is available \citep[art.~77]{brasil1973lei}. Abolition did not change how deaths are recorded. In a triple difference like the one below, neither the share of land-transport deaths that occur on the road (half of them) nor the share of road deaths without a clock time moves with abolition (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:records}).

\subsection{Crashes on federal highways}

The Federal Highway Police (Pol\'icia Rodovi\'aria Federal, PRF) publish as open data every crash they attend on federal highways, from 2007 to 2025, with date, clock time, municipality, numbers of dead and injured, type of crash and the light conditions the officer observed: full daylight, dawn, dusk or night \citep{prf2025dados}. I use two outcomes. Federal highway deaths count people dead at the scene of the crash \citep{prf2025anuario}, the same concept as road deaths in the SIM. Federal highway injury crashes are crashes with at least one dead or injured person. Crashes without victims are not used: an online self-report gradually replaced police attendance for them, at different dates in different states, which breaks that series differently in the two groups. The two registers overlap only in part. Road deaths cover every public road, urban streets included; federal highways are a network of intercity roads, mostly outside cities, which carried 1,176 deaths per summer in the treated states before abolition, against 2,382 road deaths (Table~\ref{tab:descriptives}).

\subsection{Traffic counts}

The National Traffic Count Plan (Plano Nacional de Contagem de Tr\'afego, PNCT) of the federal roads agency (DNIT) publishes hourly vehicle counts, by direction and vehicle class, at continuous counting stations on federal highways \citep{dnit2025pnct}. I use complete station-days counted from 2014 to May 2019 and from May 2021 to 2025, which cover the summers 2014/15 to 2018/19 and 2021/22 to 2024/25.\footnote{DNIT's contract for continuous counts ended in June 2019. The values published for the second half of 2019 were estimated with a statistical model, and nothing was counted in 2020 \citep[p.~7]{dnit2020nota}. A new contract was tendered in 2020 \citep{dnit2020edital} and signed on 30 December 2020 and 13 January 2021; counting resumed in May 2021. I drop every station-day from June 2019 to December 2020, and any station-day whose daily total repeats exactly on the same weekday one to four weeks apart, which marks a modelled value.} The new contract replaced the equipment, and no station is counted both before and after abolition.

\subsection{Sun and clock}

For each municipal seat and day I compute sunrise and sunset in standard time from the solar position equations of \citet{noaa2025solar}, using the seat coordinates from IBGE and the standard offset of the municipality's time zone. Every death and crash is then placed in a 60-minute bin of clock time relative to standard-time sunset or sunrise at its municipality on its date. The full solar algorithm \citep{meeus1998astronomical} moves sunset by at most 1.6 minutes and the main estimate from 29.2 to 29.8 log points (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}). The death certificates and the federal highway police records both give legal clock time, the time on the clock under whatever regime was in force; Section~\ref{sec:firststage} shows this in the officers' records, and Online Appendix~\ref{app:data} does so for the traffic counts.

\subsection{Sample}

The treated group consists of the 10 states with DST in every summer from 2008/09 to 2018/19 and the Federal District, which contains the capital, Bras\'ilia, and has the powers of a state. I refer to these 11 units as the treated states. The control group is the 12 states of the North and Northeast without DST: Rond\^onia, Roraima, Par\'a, Amap\'a, Maranh\~ao, Piau\'i, Cear\'a, Rio Grande do Norte, Para\'iba, Pernambuco, Alagoas and Sergipe. I exclude Bahia and Tocantins, which had DST in one summer each, and Acre and Amazonas, which changed time zone during the sample (Figure~\ref{fig:map}). A season runs from July to June, so that each summer falls within one season, and is named by its first year. The sample runs from 2008/09, the first season under the 2008 decree, to 2023/24, the last for which the death register is final, so it has 11 seasons with DST and 5 without.

The summer window runs from 15 November to 14 February. It is the set of days that were under DST in every season before abolition: the latest start of DST in the sample was 4 November 2018 and the earliest end 15 February 2009. The same window is used in every season, before and after abolition, so no day in it is partly treated and the year-to-year variation in DST dates does not enter the comparison. The window starts at least 11 days after the latest start of DST and ends before the earliest end, so the weeks around clock changes, when the literature finds the effects of lost sleep \citep{smith2016spring, gillmore2025daylight}, fall outside it. The off-season runs from 1 April to 31 August, when no state ever had DST. The estimation panel has one row per state and day in these two windows: 23 states and 245 days in each of 16 seasons, or 90,160 state-days.

In the treated states, road deaths in hour 0 rose from 110 to 141 per summer after abolition, while those in the same hour of the off-season fell from 362 to 313; in the control states both fell. In log points these changes combine to about 29 (33 percent). Pedestrian deaths in hour 0 of the treated states' summer doubled, from 13 to 27 per summer, while they fell in the off-season and in the control states.

\section{Empirical Strategy}\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Specification}

For each state $s$ and day $d$ in the summer window or the off-season, let $y_{sd}$ count the events that occur in one hour bin, hour 0 unless stated otherwise. The main specification is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main}
  y_{sd} = \exp\big(\beta\, T_s W_d A_d + \alpha_{s,w(d)} + \gamma_{s,t(d)} + \delta_d\big)\,\varepsilon_{sd},
\end{equation}
where $T_s$ marks the 11 treated states, $W_d$ days in the summer window and $A_d$ seasons after abolition. The fixed effects are state by window ($\alpha$; summer window or off-season), state by season ($\gamma$) and date ($\delta$). I report $100\beta$, the effect in log points.

Each set of fixed effects removes one threat. State-by-window effects absorb every permanent difference between a state's summer and its off-season: tourism, the rainy season, and the fact that hour 0 falls at a later clock time in summer than in winter. State-by-season effects absorb anything that moves a state's counts in both windows of a season, such as its vehicle fleet, enforcement or the pandemic. Date effects absorb national holidays and national shocks. What remains to identify $\beta$ is the change, after abolition, in the gap between the summer and the off-season of the treated states, relative to the same change in the control states. The identifying assumption is that, without abolition, that gap would have moved in parallel in the two groups.

I estimate equation~(\ref{eq:main}) by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood, which requires only that the conditional mean be correct and handles the many zeros of a single hour's count \citep{santossilva2006log}: 88 percent of state-days have no road death in hour 0. The share of zeros implied by the fitted means matches the observed share within one percentage point in every outcome, and the ratio of the residual variance to the mean is between 0.9 and 1.6, so neither a zero-inflated nor a negative binomial model is needed. % inference.rds: zeros_obs_pct against zeros_poisson_pct; dispersion 0.93 to 1.57.

\subsection{Why one hour}

The design takes its force from the hour. Within the summer window alone, standard-time sunset differs across Brazilian municipalities by almost two hours, so a fixed block of clock hours mixes the hour whose light flipped with hours whose light did not and dilutes the effect. The switched hour also tells in advance where an effect of light must appear and where it must not. A shock to the treated states' summers unrelated to light, such as a change in policing, has no reason to concentrate in the hour that follows standard-time sunset at each municipality on each date and to spare the hours on either side of it.

\subsection{Inference}

Standard errors are clustered by state. With 23 clusters, 11 of them treated, cluster-robust inference can over-reject \citep{cameron2008bootstrap}, so I report two further p-values. The first is from a wild cluster bootstrap with the null imposed, Webb weights and 9,999 draws \citep{webb2023reworking}, applied to the linear analogue of equation~(\ref{eq:main}) estimated by least squares on counts. The second is from permutation inference. I assign the treatment to 11 of the 23 states drawn at random, 999 times, and re-estimate the Poisson model. The p-value is the share of draws, counting the actual assignment, whose t-statistic is at least as large in absolute value as the actual one. The test compares t-statistics rather than estimates because states differ widely in size, and with heterogeneous clusters a test on the estimate can be unreliable while one on the t-statistic typically does better \citep{mackinnon2020randomization}. DST was not assigned at random, so the test asks whether an arbitrary group of 11 states would produce an estimate as large as the one the treated states produce.

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}

\subsection{The hour turned dark}\label{sec:firststage}

Panel B of Figure~\ref{fig:light} shows that the switched hour turned dark in the officers' records, and that the records use legal clock time. For crashes in the treated states' summer window, it plots the share recorded at dusk or night by 10-minute bin of clock time relative to standard-time sunset. Under DST, half of the crashes were recorded at dusk or night by standard-time sunset; without DST, half are by 50 minutes before it. The curve moved by close to the hour the clock moved, which is what legal clock time implies. In hour 0, the share recorded at dusk or night rose by 23.6 percentage points (standard error 2.0) in a linear version of the triple difference of equation~(\ref{eq:main}), from 74 percent before abolition. % light_dose.rds, first_stage: fs_pp, fs_se_pp, treated_pre_dark_pct.
The record is a coarse measure of light. Officers recorded many crashes in the last hour of sunlight as dusk, so the 24 points understate the change from sun above the horizon to sun below it.\footnote{Dividing the effect on road deaths in Table~\ref{tab:main} by this change gives 124 log points for an hour that goes from fully light to fully dark (95 percent interval 42 to 197; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:dose}). The ratio treats the officers' record as the dose of darkness and inherits its error.}

\subsection{Deaths in the hour that turned dark}

Panel A of Table~\ref{tab:main} reports the main estimates. In the hour that turned dark, road deaths rose by 29.2 log points (standard error 9.0), or 34 percent. Federal highway deaths rose by 53.9 log points (20.3) and federal highway injury crashes by 22.2 (5.6). The permutation p-values are 0.018, 0.014 and 0.007, and the wild bootstrap p-values on the linear model 0.010, 0.002 and 0.001. In the treated states, hour 0 had 110 road deaths per summer before abolition; after it, observed deaths exceed the counterfactual by 36 per summer in that hour alone, before any offset elsewhere in the day. % reallocation.rds, hours: eve+0 excess_per_season 35.6 (se 9.5).

Panel B reports the morning hour, which turned light. All three estimates are negative and small relative to their standard errors: $-3.3$ log points (12.4) for road deaths, $-11.3$ (20.4) for federal highway deaths and $-14.2$ (8.3) for injury crashes. Light gained in the morning lowered deaths far less than light lost in the evening raised them, although the two hours had about as many road deaths before abolition (107 and 110 per summer).

Figure~\ref{fig:hours} estimates equation~(\ref{eq:main}) hour by hour around sunset and sunrise. In all three outcomes the estimate peaks at hour 0. For road deaths, the next hour, which went from twilight to night, also rises (16.4 log points, standard error 11.2), and no other hour moves much. Federal highways show one more feature: crashes in the hour before sunset fall ($-22.3$ log points for injury crashes). Section~\ref{sec:trends} shows that this fall began in 2018/19, the last summer with DST, before abolition.

Hour 0 is the 60 minutes after standard-time sunset (left) or sunrise (right), the hour that turned dark or light; hour $-1$ is the 60 minutes before.

\subsection{Trends and robustness}\label{sec:trends}

\begin{figure}[tbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics{fig_event_study.pdf}
  \caption{The Hour after Sunset and the Hour before, Season by Season}
  \label{fig:event-study}
  \begin{figurenotes}[Notes]
  Equation~(\ref{eq:main}) with $T_s W_d$ interacted with each season instead of with $A_d$; 2018/19, the last season with DST, is the reference. 95 percent confidence intervals, standard errors clustered by state. The shaded seasons had no DST.
  \end{figurenotes}
  \begin{figurenotes}[Sources]
  \citet{datasus2025sim}; \citet{prf2025dados}.
  \end{figurenotes}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:event-study} replaces the single post-abolition indicator with one coefficient per season, measured against 2018/19, for hour 0 and the hour before it. For road deaths, the coefficients before abolition show no trend (a slope of $-0.5$ log points per season, standard error 2.1) and are jointly indistinguishable from zero ($p=0.18$). % pretrends.rds: pre_trend_lp, pre_trend_se, wald_pre_p.
The reference season was a high one: the earlier seasons average $-15$ log points against it. Each of the five seasons without DST lies above that average, the first two by the most. For federal highway injury crashes the earlier coefficients drift upward ($p<0.001$ for the joint test), and the hour before sunset was already low in 2018/19 relative to every earlier season, so its fall after abolition predates abolition. % switched_hour_event_study.rds: PRF injury crashes, hour -1, 2008/09-2017/18 between 24.9 and 55.5 log points against 2018/19.

\begin{table}[tbp]
  \caption{The Hour after Sunset under Other Choices, and Hours Whose Light Did Not Change}
  \label{tab:robustness}
  \centering\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{5pt}
  \input{\tabdir/tab_robustness.tex}
  \begin{tablenotes}[Notes]
  Panel A: equation~(\ref{eq:main}) with one change per row; standard errors clustered by state. The state-by-day row compares hour 0 with hours 3 to 5 before and 2 to 4 after sunset of the same state and day. The joint test is a Wald test that the ten season coefficients before 2018/19 in Figure~\ref{fig:event-study} are zero. Panel B: counterfactual fitted on untreated state-days only, with week and day-of-week effects in place of date effects; 95 percent intervals in brackets, from 299 draws of a state bootstrap. Panel C: midday is at least three hours after sunrise and more than three hours before sunset; night is at least three hours after sunset or more than two hours before sunrise.
  \end{tablenotes}
  \begin{tablenotes}[Sources]
  \citet{datasus2025sim}; \citet{prf2025dados}.
  \end{tablenotes}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:robustness} reports the checks this calls for. With a linear treated-by-summer trend fitted on all seasons, the estimate for road deaths is 39.9 log points (20.7). That trend also runs through the seasons after abolition and can absorb part of the effect. Panel B therefore uses a Poisson version of the imputation estimator of \citet{borusyak2024revisiting}, which fits the counterfactual on untreated observations only. With a trend learned before 2019 and extrapolated, road deaths rose 38 percent (95 percent interval $-12$ to 103), against 31 percent (7 to 54) without the trend. Extrapolating the trend costs precision, not effect. On federal highways the trend matters: with it, injury crashes rise by 5.6 log points (8.0) and by 8 percent ($-5$ to 26) in the imputation. I therefore read road deaths for the size of the effect, and the federal highway records for the first stage and the mechanism. Federal highways also had a shock of their own in the first summer without DST: a presidential order suspended the police's static, mobile and portable speed cameras from mid-August to 23 December 2019 \citep{brasil2019despacho, poder3602019radares}. Without that summer, the federal highway estimates are larger, not smaller (65.0 for deaths and 25.7 for injury crashes; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}). The estimate for road deaths is also stable without the pandemic seasons (31.1, standard error 8.8) and with state-by-day fixed effects that compare hour 0 with hours of the same state and day whose light did not change (27.7, 12.4). The control states kept their clocks, but schedules set on Bras\'ilia time have run an hour later on them in summer since abolition. Their evening traffic did not move, and within the treated states alone, without the control states, the same comparison gives 47.2 (7.8) (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:within-group}). No single state or season is decisive: leaving out one state at a time gives between 24.3 and 34.1, and one season at a time between 22.7 and 35.2 (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:leave-out}).

A formal sensitivity analysis in the spirit of \citet{rambachan2023more} asks less of the event study than it can give. Its target is the average post-abolition coefficient against 2018/19 alone (14.8 log points), not $\beta$, and with a single reference season that average is too imprecise to rule out small departures from a linear trend (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:honestdid}). % honestdid.rds: avg_post_lp 14.85; breakdown M 0.02.
The case for a causal reading rests on the pattern within the day: the peak in one hour defined by the local sun, the quiet neighboring hours and the hours whose light did not change, and the concentration among pedestrians.

Recorded times heap on the hour and the half hour (34.5 and 23.0 percent of road deaths). Shifting the hour 0 window by 5 to 15 minutes moves the estimate in the direction light predicts: it is larger when the window starts later and the hour is darker. Dropping every death recorded on the hour or half hour leaves 16.7 log points (12.9), with less than half the sample (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:window-shift} and Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}).

\subsection{Is it sleep?}

Two features of the design keep acute sleep loss out of the estimates: abolition involved no lost night, and the summer window excludes the weeks around clock changes. A chronic effect through the clock time of sunset \citep{giuntella2019sunset} would run the other way, since an earlier clock sunset should lengthen sleep, not shorten it. And a sleep effect would not confine itself to one hour of the day. Panel C of Table~\ref{tab:robustness} estimates equation~(\ref{eq:main}) for hours whose light did not change, midday and night. Nothing rises in them: road deaths move by $-4.5$ (5.8) and $-6.6$ (5.6) log points. Federal highway injury crashes fall at night ($-6.1$, $p=0.04$), consistent with the traffic that left the dark evening (Section~\ref{sec:traffic}).

\subsection{Who dies}

\begin{table}[tbp]
  \caption{Pedestrians and Other Road Users in the Hour after Sunset}
  \label{tab:pedestrians}
  \centering\footnotesize
  \input{\tabdir/tab_pedestrians.tex}
  \begin{tablenotes}[Notes]
  Equation~(\ref{eq:main}) for hour 0, estimated separately for events with a pedestrian victim and for all others; Panel C from one stacked model. Inference as in Table~\ref{tab:main}; in each permutation draw both members of the pair receive the same set of treated states, and the difference is divided by the square root of the sum of the two squared standard errors. Excess events are observed minus predicted without abolition, treated states, summer window, after 2019.
  \end{tablenotes}
  \begin{tablenotes}[Sources]
  \citet{datasus2025sim}; \citet{prf2025dados}.
  \end{tablenotes}
\end{table}

The increase falls mostly on pedestrians (Table~\ref{tab:pedestrians}). Pedestrian road deaths in hour 0 rose by 76.6 log points (29.8), more than doubling, while the deaths of all other road users rose by 17.9 (7.8). Pedestrians were 11.7 percent of road deaths in hour 0 before abolition and account for 43.4 percent of the excess after it. On federal highways the contrast is sharper: 170 log points for pedestrian deaths against 26 for all others. The pedestrian estimates pass the wild bootstrap and the permutation test in all three registers. The difference between pedestrians and others is significant on federal highways (permutation $p=0.001$ for deaths and for injury crashes) and borderline for road deaths ($p=0.075$).

Among the other road users, motorcyclist deaths rose by 19.6 log points (10.9) and deaths of car occupants did not change ($-0.2$, standard error 35.2). The increase was larger on weekends and holidays (41.3, 15.8) than on working days (16.1, 10.0), so it is not confined to the commute home (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:road-users}). This is the pattern visibility predicts. A pedestrian is the road user who most depends on being seen, and pedestrian crash risk is the most sensitive to ambient light around the clock changes \citep{sullivan2002role}; pedestrian deaths at night also fall on brighter moonlit nights \citep{tyndall2025road}. It is also hard to reconcile with sleep, which would impair drivers whoever they hit. Street lighting points the same way without precision: splitting the municipalities of each state at the median share of households on unlit streets, the estimate is 40.8 log points (10.3) in the darker half and 14.1 (15.6) in the better-lit half ($p=0.16$ for the difference; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:lighting}).

\subsection{Traffic followed the light}\label{sec:traffic}

Drivers adapted to the new light. Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:volume} estimates equation~(\ref{eq:main}) on hourly vehicle counts at federal highway stations. After abolition, traffic in the treated states' summer fell by 6.4 log points (2.2) in hour 0 and by 5.1 (1.3) in the hour before it, and rose by 11.7 (5.0) in the morning hour that turned light, with permutation p-values of 0.069, 0.025 and 0.159. Subtracting the volume estimate from the crash estimate gives the change in crashes per vehicle. In hour 0, injury crashes per vehicle rose by 28.6 log points ($p=0.002$), more than crashes themselves; in the morning hour that turned light they fell by 26.0 ($p=0.009$). Fewer vehicles travel in the dark hour, and each faces a higher risk. Two caveats apply. The stations cover federal highways only and say nothing about urban traffic, where many of the pedestrian deaths in the death register occur. And the volume and crash estimates come from overlapping but different sets of summers, since the stations did not count in the first two summers without DST.

\subsection{The morning does not pay for the evening}

\begin{table}[tbp]
  \caption{Excess Events per Summer after Abolition}
  \label{tab:excess}
  \centering\footnotesize
  \input{\tabdir/tab_excess.tex}
  \begin{tablenotes}[Notes]
  Events per summer in the treated states after abolition minus those predicted without it, from one model that stacks seven hours (two before to two after standard-time sunset; one before to two after standard-time sunrise) with every fixed effect of equation~(\ref{eq:main}) interacted with the hour. Delta-method standard errors in parentheses. The whole day comes from a separate model. Only events with a recorded clock time, so the counts understate the events in each hour.
  \end{tablenotes}
  \begin{tablenotes}[Sources]
  \citet{datasus2025sim}; \citet{prf2025dados}.
  \end{tablenotes}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:excess} turns the estimates into events per summer: observed counts in the treated states' summers after abolition minus those predicted without it. The seven hours around sunset and sunrise enter one stacked model, with every fixed effect interacted with the hour, so that their excess counts can be summed with the right covariance. The two evening hours that turned darker added 57 road deaths per summer (standard error 19), and the morning hour that turned light removed 3 (11). Net, abolition added 54 road deaths per summer (20), 17 percent of the deaths predicted in these three hours ($p=0.007$). % reallocation.rds, sums: 54.23, se 20.06, pct_of_cf 17.3, p 0.0069.
Across all seven hours around sunset and sunrise, including those whose light changed only in degree, the net is 41 (41). Estimated directly, the whole day gives $-5$ deaths (66). That estimate adds the variation of every hour of the day to an effect concentrated in three, so its standard error exceeds the evening effect. The whole-day count can therefore neither confirm the net figure nor rule it out, and I do not read it as evidence that abolition only moved deaths between hours of the day.

On federal highways the net is positive in the hours whose light changed, 29 deaths (14) and 93 injury crashes (43) per summer. Across all seven hours it is close to zero for deaths and negative for injury crashes, because of the hours before sunset whose decline, as shown above, predates abolition.

The size of the effect is in line with earlier estimates. In the three hours whose light changed, abolition added 17 percent to the predicted count of road deaths; \citet{coate2004effects} estimate that year-round DST in the United States would lower pedestrian deaths by 13 percent and occupant deaths by 3 percent in the morning and evening periods it affects. That pedestrians drive the increase matches evidence that their crash risk in the dark is up to seven times that in daylight \citep{sullivan2002role}. In absolute terms, \citet{smith2016spring} attributes more than 30 deaths a year to the spring transition in the United States, a population more than twice the 131 million affected here; the darker evenings of a permanent regime cost more lives than that in a single summer.

\section{What Abolition Cost}\label{sec:cost}

\begin{table}[tbp]
  \caption{Deaths per Summer and What They Are Worth}
  \label{tab:cost}
  \centering\footnotesize
  \input{\tabdir/tab_cost.tex}
  \begin{tablenotes}[Notes]
  Panel A: excess deaths per summer in the two hours after standard-time sunset and the hour after standard-time sunrise (Table~\ref{tab:excess}). Column 1 is the estimate. Column 2 adds road deaths without a clock time, assuming they occur in these hours in the same proportion as deaths with one. Column 3 adds deaths off the road, 85 percent of them in hospital, under the same assumption; it is an extrapolation. Shares are of all land-transport deaths in the treated states' summer window before abolition. Panel B: value of a statistical life (VSL) by the reference approach of \citet{robinson2019valuing}, from gross national income per head at purchasing-power parity in 2025, converted to reais at the 2025 PPP rate; and the Ipea social cost of a death on a federal highway, a human-capital cost that excludes the value of life itself (December 2014 prices brought to December 2025 by the IPCA). Delta-method standard errors in parentheses.
  \end{tablenotes}
  \begin{tablenotes}[Sources]
  \citet{worldbank2026wdi}; \citet{ipea2015acidentes}; \citet{ibge2026ipca}.
  \end{tablenotes}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:cost} scales and values the net count. Column 1 is the estimate, 54 deaths per summer in the three hours whose light changed, the two after standard-time sunset and the one after standard-time sunrise (Table~\ref{tab:excess}); they are 0.9 percent of all land-transport deaths in the treated states' summer window. Column 2 assumes that road deaths without a recorded time fall in these three hours in the same proportion as those with one, which gives 67. Column 3 also assumes that deaths off the road, 85 percent of them in hospital, follow deaths on the road in proportion, which gives 137; it is an extrapolation, because the design cannot place a death in hospital in the hour of its crash.

I value a death with the reference rule of \citet{robinson2019valuing} for transferring a value of a statistical life (VSL) to a lower-income country: the US ratio of VSL to income per head, 160, extrapolated to Brazil with an income elasticity of 1.5, so that $\mathit{VSL}_{\mathit{BR}} = 160\, Y_{\mathit{US}}\, (Y_{\mathit{BR}}/Y_{\mathit{US}})^{1.5}$, where $Y$ is gross national income per head at purchasing power parity in 2025 \citep{worldbank2026wdi}. The resulting VSL is 1.8 million international dollars, or R\$4.7 million at the 2025 parity rate (Online Appendix~\ref{app:cost} gives the inputs and the alternative rules). % total_cost.rds, vsl: 1,825,618 international dollars; R$ 4.66338 million.
At that value, the estimated deaths cost R\$253 million per summer in 2025 reais (standard error 94), and R\$637 million under the broadest scaling. The two alternative rules of \citet{robinson2019valuing} give larger values, up to R\$1.3 billion. A human-capital valuation of a death on a federal highway \citep{ipea2015acidentes}, which leaves out the value of life itself, gives R\$43 to 108 million.

The energy side of the ledger has changed sign over time. The technical note behind the 2019 decision estimated that DST had raised electricity load by about 0.7 percent \citep{mme2019nota}; on that estimate, abolition saved a little electricity at the price of the deaths in the darkened evenings. For today's system, the grid operator estimates that reinstating DST would save R\$244 to 356 million in thermal-generation fuel in one summer and, by lowering the evening peak by about 2 GW, about R\$1.8 billion a year in payments for reserve capacity \citep{ons2024nota}. These figures come from a different method and are not strictly comparable with the ones here. On them, the two sides of the ledger now point the same way: reinstating DST would save fuel worth about as much as the reference value of the deaths in column 1, and capacity payments that, if realized, are larger. Neither side counts the two clock changes a year that abolition removed, whose cost the literature attributes to lost sleep in the days after the spring change \citep{smith2016spring, gillmore2025daylight}; the summer window excludes those weeks, so this paper does not measure it.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{A Second Abolition: Mexico}\label{sec:mexico}

Mexico abolished DST under the Ley de los Husos Horarios, which took effect on 30 October 2022 \citep{mexico2022ley}. Before then, most of the country advanced its clocks from the first Sunday of April to the last Sunday of October. The law kept a seasonal clock, on US dates, in Baja California and in 22 municipalities on the border with the United States in Coahuila, Nuevo Le\'on and Tamaulipas; Sonora and Quintana Roo had no DST before the law and kept their clocks. Chihuahua, which the same law moved to another time zone, is left out (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:map-mexico}).

The national statistics office (INEGI) records the traffic accidents on roads outside federal jurisdiction in its register of land traffic accidents in urban and suburban areas (Accidentes de Tr\'ansito Terrestre en Zonas Urbanas y Suburbanas, ATUS), with its date, clock time and municipality, and the dead at the scene by type of road user \citep{inegi2026atus}. I build hour 0 as in Brazil, from the municipal seat \citep{inegi2026marco} and the standard time zone, with a summer window from 8 April to 24 October, under DST in every year from 2016 to 2022 in the areas that lost it, and an off-season from 8 November to 7 March. The sample runs from 2016 to 2025, seven summers with DST and three without. Nearly every accident in the sample has a recorded time, and the hourly profile of accidents shows that the record uses legal clock time (Online Appendix~\ref{app:mexico}).

The comparison group is the weak point. The six units that kept their clocks are small and record few deaths in hour 0. A triple difference against them gives a large estimate for hour 0 (80.8 log points, standard error 19.8) together with an implausible one for the hour before sunset, whose light changed only in degree ($-126.3$, 41.3; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:mexico}, Panels A and B). I therefore rely on a comparison that does not use them. Panel D compares, within each unit that lost DST and each day, hour 0 with the hours whose light did not change, 3 to 5 hours before sunset and 2 to 4 after, in the summer window against the off-season, after abolition against before, with fixed effects for each unit and day. It shows the Brazilian signature. Deaths at the scene in hour 0 rose by 58.4 log points (17.6), pedestrian deaths by 142.8 (37.8), and accidents with a pedestrian struck by 44.9 (7.6). The morning hour that turned light shows the mirror image among pedestrians, a fall of 42.4 log points (18.2) in accidents with a pedestrian struck (Panel C).

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

When Brazil stopped moving its clocks, the evening hour that lost its sunlight became deadlier on the road, mostly for pedestrians, and the morning hour that gained light did not compensate. Counting only deaths at the scene with a recorded time, abolition cost 54 lives per summer in the hours whose light changed. The same signature appears in Mexico's abolition three years later.

The estimates have limits that matter for their use. They count deaths in the hours whose light changed, and understate even those, since they leave out deaths off the road, deaths without a recorded time and all nonfatal injuries. They come from 23 states and five summers without DST, two of them in the pandemic. The whole-day effect is estimated too imprecisely to say whether some deaths moved to other hours, and the federal highway records are sensitive to a pre-existing trend. The traffic counts cover only federal highways.

For Brazil, the estimates answer the policy question directly: bringing seasonal DST back or forbidding it is the comparison the paper measures, and Section~\ref{sec:cost} puts the lives on the same ledger as the energy. Elsewhere the numbers travel less far. In summer, seasonal and permanent DST set the same clock, so the estimates are the cost, in summer evenings, of choosing permanent standard time over either. They say nothing about winter, when permanent DST would darken the mornings, least of all at latitudes higher than Brazil's, and they do not weigh the clock changes, energy use or the chronic effects of the clock on sleep. Part of what people did to protect themselves, driving less in the dark hour, is already in the estimates. Within these limits, darker evenings cost lives on the road that brighter mornings do not return, and those lives are mostly pedestrians, whom street lighting and road design can protect when the clock does not.
